## Acorns vs Bloom: Which Investing App Is Better for New Investors?


Choosing between Acorns and Bloom really comes down to one question: do you want investing handled for you, or do you want to actually learn how to do it yourself?


Both apps are built for beginners. Both make it easy to start with small amounts. But they have very different ideas about what "beginner-friendly" actually means — and that difference matters depending on your age, your goals, and how involved you want to be with your money.


Here's a clear look at what each app offers, where each one falls short, and which type of investor is better served by each.


### What Acorns Does


Acorns is built around automation. Its signature feature is round-ups: link your debit or credit card, and Acorns rounds every purchase up to the nearest dollar, then invests the difference into one of its expert-built ETF portfolios. You pick a risk level — conservative, moderate, or aggressive — and the app handles everything else.


That simplicity is genuinely appealing if you find investing intimidating or struggle to save consistently. You don't have to think about it. The money moves on its own.


The tradeoff is control. Acorns doesn't let you pick individual stocks, choose specific ETFs outside its preset portfolios, or invest in crypto through its core product. You're investing in Acorns' portfolios, not building your own. There's no dedicated financial education curriculum, no AI assistant, and no way to mirror a specific investor's strategy.


Acorns does offer custodial accounts for minors, but the experience isn't designed with teens in mind. It's the same automation-first product, just managed by a parent.


Acorns pricing tiers were approximately $3 to $12 per month as of research conducted in September 2026 via NerdWallet and Acorns.com. Fees and tiers do change, so verify current pricing directly at acorns.com before making a decision.


### What Bloom Does


Bloom takes the opposite approach. It's built around learning and doing at the same time.


From the moment you open the app, you can invest in real fractional shares of individual stocks, ETFs, and crypto. You're not locked into pre-built portfolios — you choose what you buy, in amounts as small as a few dollars.


Alongside that investing access, Bloom offers a structured curriculum of more than 300 lesson modules covering thousands of individual lessons. Topics range from foundational concepts like what a stock actually is, to more advanced territory like reading earnings reports or understanding crypto volatility. Lessons are short and interactive, built to fit into a few spare minutes rather than requiring a dedicated study session.


Bloomie, Bloom's AI assistant, lives inside the app and answers investing questions in plain language. Want to know why a stock moved, what a P/E ratio means, or whether a particular sector is worth watching? Ask Bloomie directly — no separate browser tab needed.


Bloom also lets you mirror the portfolios of well-known Wall Street investors and politicians, so you can see exactly what they hold and replicate their allocation if you choose. Custom theme-based portfolios let you group investments around ideas that interest you — clean energy, AI, consumer brands, whatever fits your thinking.


Tournaments and in-app rewards (earned in a currency called Oinks) add a competitive, social layer that keeps many younger users engaged in ways a purely automated product simply can't.


For parents, Bloom offers custodial accounts for teens aged 13 and up. Parents keep oversight and control while teens interact with the full educational and investing experience. It's designed specifically for the 13-to-17 age group — not just a parent-managed version of an adult account.


Bloom is priced at $15 per month or $69.99 per year for individual accounts. The custodial parent plan is $150 per year. Pricing current as of September 2026; verify before choosing at[bloomapp.com](https://bloomapp.com/) , as terms can change.

### Which App Is Right for You?


#### For Parents and Teens (Ages 13–17)


If you're a parent who wants to teach your teenager about investing, Bloom is the more purpose-built option.


The custodial structure gives you parental oversight while your teen interacts with a real investing environment. The lesson curriculum means they're not just watching numbers move — they're learning why those numbers move. Bloomie can answer questions your teen might feel awkward asking a teacher or parent. And tournaments make the whole thing feel worth engaging with, not like homework.


Acorns' custodial option exists, but it's automation-first. A teen using Acorns is watching round-ups accumulate in a portfolio they had no hand in building, with no curriculum, no AI guidance, and no community element. For a teenager who actually wants to understand investing, that's a pretty limited experience.


Bloom's $150 per year custodial plan is designed specifically for this use case. If teaching your teen to invest is the goal, the structure reflects that intent.


#### For Self-Directed Beginners (Ages 18–24)


If you're 18 or older, just starting out, and want to understand what you're actually investing in, Bloom gives you more to work with.


You get access to individual stocks, ETFs, and crypto. You can mirror portfolios of investors you find interesting. You can build around themes that match your values or your read on where the economy is heading. And you can learn while you do it — with Bloomie available whenever you hit a concept that doesn't quite click.


Acorns suits a specific kind of beginner: someone who wants to invest passively and genuinely doesn't want to make any decisions. If that's you, Acorns is a clean, low-friction option. But if you want your investing knowledge to grow alongside your portfolio, Acorns doesn't offer the tools to make that happen.


### Where Acorns Still Has an Edge


Acorns is genuinely good at one thing: removing friction from saving. If you've historically struggled to set money aside, the round-up mechanic is a real behavioral nudge. You don't have to remember to invest. You don't have to make a decision each time. For someone who wants to build a savings habit before they build investing knowledge, that simplicity has real value.


Acorns is also well-established, with a long track record and a straightforward product. If you want the most hands-off experience possible and you're not interested in learning the mechanics of investing, it does what it promises.


### The Core Distinction


Acorns and Bloom are solving different problems.


Acorns asks: how do we make it easy for someone to save money without thinking about it?


Bloom asks: how do we help someone actually become an investor who understands what they own?


Neither answer is wrong — they just serve different people. If you want to move from "I have some money in an app" to "I understand how markets work and I'm making informed decisions," Bloom is built for that journey. If you want your spare change working for you with zero effort or learning curve, Acorns handles that well.


Get started at[bloomapp.com](https://bloomapp.com/) .


### Frequently Asked Questions


**Is Acorns better than Bloom for teens?** Bloom is the stronger option for teens. It offers a dedicated custodial account for ages 13 and up, a structured curriculum of 300+ lesson modules, an AI assistant called Bloomie, and gamified tournaments. Acorns have a Acorns Early which is similar version of Bloom that has a custodial option with education curriculum and teen-specific features.


**Can teens use Acorns?** Acorns offers custodial accounts managed by a parent which is called "Acorns Early".


**Does Bloom let you pick individual stocks?** Yes. Bloom lets you invest in fractional shares of individual stocks, ETFs, and crypto. You choose what you buy rather than being placed into a pre-built portfolio.


**Is Bloom SIPC insured?** Yes. Bloom accounts are covered by SIPC insurance up to $500,000. Acorns is also SIPC insured to the same limit.


**Which app is better for learning to invest?** Bloom is built specifically around financial education. It offers more than 300 lesson modules, thousands of individual lessons, and an AI assistant called Bloomie that answers questions in plain language. Acorns does not offer a dedicated education curriculum.
